Build a small command-line tool in this empty folder: a habit tracker in Python 3.9, standard library only.

It runs as `python -m habits [--file PATH] COMMAND ...`. Data is kept in a JSON file: PATH from --file, else the
HABITS_FILE environment variable, else `habits.json` in the current directory. A missing file means no habits yet.

Commands (output goes to stdout, errors to stderr):
- `add NAME`: add a habit; prints `added NAME`. If it exists already: `error: NAME exists`, exit code 1.
- `done NAME [--date YYYY-MM-DD]`: mark the habit done on that day (default: today); prints `NAME done YYYY-MM-DD`.
  Marking the same day twice keeps one entry.
- `list`: one line per habit, sorted by name: the name, two spaces, the number of distinct days it was done.
  No habits: prints nothing.
- `streak NAME [--today YYYY-MM-DD]`: prints the current streak, the number of consecutive days done that end on
  today, or on yesterday when today is not done yet; otherwise 0.
- `remove NAME`: delete the habit; prints `removed NAME`.
For `done`, `streak` and `remove`, an unknown habit prints `error: no habit NAME`, exit code 1.
A date that is not a valid YYYY-MM-DD prints `error: bad date VALUE`, exit code 2.
Exit code 0 otherwise. Write unit tests for it as you go.

Build a command-line tool in this empty folder: csv2json, in Python 3.9, standard library only. It is a package
`csv2json` that runs as `python -m csv2json` and also offers `convert(text, types=False, key=None, delimiter=",")`,
importable as `from csv2json import convert`, which takes CSV text and returns JSON text.

- The first row is the header. By default the output is a JSON array with one object per data row, keys in header
  order, every value a string.
- `types=True` (`--types`): an empty field becomes null; `true` / `false` in any case become booleans; an integer
  (optional `-`, digits, no leading zero unless it is just `0`) becomes a number; a decimal written as digits, a dot
  and digits (optional `-`, e.g. `-1.5`, `2.0`) becomes a float; everything else stays a string.
- `key=COL` (`--key COL`): the output is an object that maps each row's COL value to the rest of that row (the COL
  field left out), in row order. A COL value seen twice is an error `duplicate key VALUE`; a COL that is not in the
  header is an error `no column COL`.
- A row with fewer fields than the header gets the missing ones as "" (null with types); a row with more fields is an
  error `row N has M fields, expected K` (N counts data rows from 1).
- Blank lines are skipped. A UTF-8 byte order mark at the start of the input is ignored.
- The JSON text is `json.dumps(value, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)` plus one newline at the end.
- Errors: convert raises ValueError with the message; the command prints `error: MESSAGE` to stderr, exit code 1.

Command line: `python -m csv2json [INPUT] [-o OUTPUT] [--types] [--key COL] [--delimiter CHAR]`. INPUT is a file
path, or standard input when it is missing or `-`; the JSON goes to OUTPUT or to standard output. Files are UTF-8.
Write unit tests for it as you go.

Build a small tic-tac-toe game library with a command-line tool in this empty folder, in Python 3.9, standard library
only: a package `ttt` with the modules `ttt.board`, `ttt.ai` and a command line `python -m ttt`.

A board is a string of 9 characters, `X`, `O` or `.`, row by row (cells 0-8, cell 0 top left, cell 8 bottom right).
X always moves first.

`ttt.board`:
- `parse(text)`: the board after removing spaces, newlines and `/`; ValueError unless 9 characters of `XO.` remain.
- `winner(board)`: `"X"` or `"O"` when that player has three in a row (row, column or diagonal), else None.
- `turn(board)`: `"X"` when both have the same number of marks, `"O"` when X has one more; any other count is a
  ValueError("illegal board"). A board where both players have three in a row is also illegal.
- `moves(board)`: the empty cells in ascending order; `[]` when the game is over (a winner, or a full board).
- `play(board, cell)`: the new board with the mark of the player to move in that cell; ValueError for a cell outside
  0-8, an occupied cell, or a finished game.
- `status(board)`: one of `"X wins"`, `"O wins"`, `"draw"`, `"X to move"`, `"O to move"`.

`ttt.ai`:
- `best_move(board)`: the cell for the player to move, by perfect play (minimax). Score a finished game from the
  mover's point of view as 10 - d for a win and d - 10 for a loss, where d is the number of moves from the current
  board to the end of the game, and 0 for a draw; pick the cell with the highest score, and the lowest cell number
  among equal scores. ValueError when the game is over. It must answer for the empty board in under 2 seconds.

`python -m ttt BOARD` prints the board as three lines of three characters, then the status line, then
`best: N` when the game is not over. `python -m ttt --selfplay` plays best_move against itself from the empty board
and prints each board after a move (one 9-character line per move), then the final status. A bad board prints
`error: MESSAGE` to stderr with exit code 1. Write unit tests for it as you go.
